summary.en: Zoom into each sign. Learn what divisional charts are, how the navamsa (D9) is built and read, what vargottama means, and why every varga needs an accurate birth time.

outcome.en: explain divisional charts and read the basics of the navamsa

question.en: A graha is at Karka 2°. What is its navamsa sign?

explanation.en: Karka is a water sign, so its navamsas start from Karka. 2° falls in the first 3°20′, so the navamsa is Karka itself: the graha is vargottama.

question.en: Why do divisional charts depend on an accurate birth time?

options.en: They are counted from the weekday
Their slices are small, so the lagna crosses them in minutes
They use the Sun's sign only
They change only once a year

explanation.en: Vargas divide each sign into small parts. The lagna moves through a D9 part in about 13 minutes on average, so a small time error can change the chart.

body.en: A varga, or divisional chart, divides each 30° sign into equal parts. Each part is given a sign of its own, and placing every graha by its part builds a new chart.
The chart you already know is D1, the rashi chart: one part per sign, so each graha simply sits in its sign. Every other varga is read alongside D1, never instead of it.
Parashara describes sixteen vargas, the shodasha vargas: D1, D2, D3, D4, D7, D9, D10, D12, D16, D20, D24, D27, D30, D40, D45 and D60. The number tells how many parts each sign gets.
Each varga looks closely at one area of life. Traditionally D9 for marriage and dharma, D10 for career, D7 for children, D12 for parents, D4 for home and property.
A simple rule: D1 shows what the chart promises; the vargas confirm, refine or qualify it. A varga rarely overturns a clear D1 picture, so start from D1 every time.

explanation.en: D1 is the rashi chart: each sign is one part, so every graha simply sits in its sign. All vargas are read alongside it.

question.en: In D10, what does the number 10 tell you?

options.en: Each sign is split into 10 parts
It is read from the 10th house only

explanation.en: The number of a varga is how many parts each sign is divided into. D10 splits each sign into ten parts of 3°.

question.en: How should vargas be used with D1?

options.en: They confirm and refine what D1 shows
They are read only when D1 is unclear

explanation.en: D1 shows the promise. Vargas zoom into particular areas and confirm, refine or qualify it.

body.en: The navamsa, D9, divides each sign into nine parts of 3°20′. It is the most used varga, and many astrologers read it beside D1 in every chart.
The navamsas of a sign are counted from a start set by its element. Fire signs start from Mesha. Earth signs from Makara. Air signs from Tula. Water signs from Karka.
A graha at Simha 8°. Simha is fire, so count from Mesha. 0°–3°20′ is Mesha, 3°20′–6°40′ Vrishabha, 6°40′–10° Mithuna. So its navamsa sign is Mithuna.
There are 27 nakshatras of 4 padas each: 108 padas. There are also 12 × 9 = 108 navamsas, each 3°20′. They match exactly: every pada is one navamsa. Ashwini pada 1 is Mesha navamsa.
The 108 navamsas run Mesha to Meena nine times around the zodiac without a break. Mesha's ninth navamsa is Dhanu, so Vrishabha's first is Makara. That's why the element rule works.
Traditionally D9 shows marriage and partnership, dharma, and the inner strength of each graha: how well it delivers what D1 promises. A graha strong in both tends to give good results.

Your Chandra is in {value}. That pada is also one navamsa, a 3°20′ slice of the sky, so your Moon's pada tells you its D9 sign. The Moon crosses a pada in about six hours, so without a birth time treat it as a best guess.

question.en: A graha is at Vrishabha 5°. What is its navamsa sign?

explanation.en: Vrishabha is an earth sign, so count from Makara. 0°–3°20′ is Makara, 3°20′–6°40′ is Kumbha. So the navamsa is Kumbha.

question.en: Air signs start their navamsa count from which sign?

explanation.en: Fire signs start from Mesha, earth from Makara, air from Tula and water from Karka.

question.en: Why does every nakshatra pada match one navamsa?

explanation.en: 27 nakshatras × 4 padas = 108, and 12 signs × 9 navamsas = 108. Each is 3°20′, so they line up exactly.

body.en: A graha is vargottama when it sits in the same sign in D1 and in D9. The word means best in the varga. It is traditionally a mark of strength.
Vargottama falls in one slice of each sign: the 1st navamsa of movable signs (0°–3°20′), the 5th of fixed signs (13°20′–16°40′) and the 9th of dual signs (26°40′–30°).
Our fictional Arjun has Shukra at Tula 2°. Tula is movable and air, so its navamsas start from Tula. 2° is the first slice, Tula again: his Shukra is vargottama.
A vargottama graha tends to give its results steadily and clearly, like a voice that says the same thing in two rooms. It adds strength, but doesn't change the graha's dignity in D1.
When the lagna is vargottama, tradition says the person tends to have a steady, well-defined sense of self. Because it depends on the lagna degree, it needs an accurate birth time.

options.en: When it is exalted in D1
When it sits in the same sign in D1 and D9
When it is in the 9th house
When it aspects its own sign

explanation.en: Vargottama means the graha's D1 sign and D9 sign are the same.

question.en: Which degree range of a fixed sign is vargottama?

explanation.en: In fixed signs the 5th navamsa, 13°20′–16°40′, repeats the sign itself. Movable signs use the 1st slice, dual signs the 9th.

question.en: A graha at Mithuna 28°: is it vargottama?

options.en: Yes, it's in the last slice of a dual sign
No, only movable signs can be
No, Mithuna has no vargottama slice

explanation.en: Mithuna is dual and air. Counting from Tula, the 9th navamsa is Mithuna, at 26°40′–30°. So 28° is vargottama.

body.en: D10 splits each sign into ten parts of 3°. It is read for career, work and public standing. Odd signs count from the sign itself; even signs from the 9th sign from it.
D2 splits each sign into two halves of 15°, and is read for wealth and resources. In Parashara's method, odd signs give Surya's half (Simha) first, then Chandra's (Karka); even signs the reverse.
D3 splits each sign into three parts of 10°: the sign itself, then the 5th and 9th signs from it. It is read for siblings, courage and initiative.
D7 splits each sign into seven parts of about 4°17′. It is read for children, creativity and what we pass on. Odd signs count from the sign itself; even signs from the 7th sign.
The finer the varga, the faster it changes. The D9 lagna shifts about every 13 minutes, the D10 lagna about every 12, the D60 lagna about every 2. A small time error can change these charts.
Your lagna is {value}. Every varga lagna comes from the lagna's exact degree, the fastest-moving point in the chart. If your time is off by 10 minutes, your D9 or D10 lagna may differ.

unknownTime.en: Without a birth time, the lagna and divisional charts can't be fixed. Your Moon's sign and nakshatra and the slow grahas' signs still hold, so lean on those.

question.en: Which varga is traditionally read for career?

explanation.en: D10, the dashamsha, splits each sign into ten parts and is read for career, work and public standing.

question.en: How many parts does D3, the drekkana, divide a sign into?

explanation.en: The drekkana splits each sign into three parts of 10°: the sign itself, then the 5th and 9th from it.

question.en: Your birth time is uncertain. What is the wisest approach?

options.en: Lean on D1 and the Moon; read vargas with care

explanation.en: Fine vargas change within minutes. With an uncertain time, the Moon-based picture and D1 signs are far more reliable.
